added.en: New `build-feature` skill (group `feature`): takes a feature from requirements to pushed code. You tick what is out of scope and approve the design and build order; then each requirement becomes a slice — just before it is built, you choose how it is tested and approve its tests — built test-first by its own sub-agent with a fresh test review, closing with a report. Needs the `commit` and `engineering` groups set up first.

New `build-feature-auto` skill (group `feature`): builds one or more features hands-off with `build-feature`'s pipeline. It asks one round of questions up front — only what no evidence answers, and whether you review after each feature or after all — decides and logs everything else, parks a feature that needs you while the run goes on, and leaves each feature as one local commit for you to push.

`commit` can keep a roadmap — now / next / later, milestones, or quarters — in the changelog file under `planned`, rendered to `ROADMAP.md`. The commit that finishes an item takes it off the roadmap and turns it into that commit's changelog entries. Set it up by asking for a roadmap, or in the commit setup.

`commit` ships a render script (needs `jq`) that prints the changelog per audience and language, one release's notes, or the roadmap as Markdown; setup can copy it into your project as `scripts/changelog.sh`.

changed.en: The `engineering-rules` testing area offers fuzzing for stacks that read untrusted input, with a `fuzz <target>` task that runs one target until coverage plateaus or its time budget (10 minutes recommended) runs out; CI fuzzes each target for a minute on every push and with the full budget nightly.
The `engineering-rules` testing area records what acceptance tests drive — entry point, fakes, what they assert on — and how end-to-end tests are structured, page objects recommended.
The `acceptance` task that `engineering-rules` sets up skips Gherkin scenarios tagged `@wip`, so scenarios written before their code keep the suite green.
The `engineering-rules` performance area offers instruction-count benchmarks: hardware-independent, so a 1% regression shows even on shared CI runners (Linux only).
The `engineering-rules` enforcement area sets up CI on Gitea Actions and Jenkins too.

The install and update scripts fetch the latest release instead of the development version on `main`; `--ref <tag>` (PowerShell: `-Ref`) installs a specific release, `--ref main` the development version.

`engineering-rules` asks what your checks must catch instead of which tools you want, plus your developer platforms and allowed runtimes, then recommends one tool per outcome and stack as a table; swap any row, each alternative shown with its comparison — convention, strengths, weak spots, adoption, speed, license.

`engineering-rules` picks the stack's built-in tool first, then its de facto standard, and only then a tool covering more ground — but a tool already in the set takes every outcome it covers, and a tool that runs the built-in one (golangci-lint runs `go vet`) counts as built-in, so the set stays small. Never a second tool for the same outcome; an installed tool duplicating another is marked for removal.

The `engineering-rules` static-analysis area asks whether agents may write code comments; `names instead` adds a `Code comments` section to your `CLAUDE.md` telling agents to use better names and extracted functions instead, keeping only comments a tool requires.

`engineering-rules` researches tools faster and with far fewer tokens: research runs on Sonnet, keeps four candidates per outcome, gathers GitHub facts in one call, researches setup details only for the tools you pick, and researches stack-independent tools (secret scanning, infrastructure, hooks, dependency updates) once for the repo.

fixed.en: `tdd-loop` squashes its checkpoints through the `commit` skill, so the squashed commit follows your project's commit convention and changelog instead of always being a Conventional Commit.
`tdd-loop`'s mutation pass runs the `mutation` command from your project's `CLAUDE.md` Testing section, so it works in projects that don't use mise.

changed.en: The `engineering-rules` testing area creates tasks to run one test file or test, report coverage for one file, and mutate only given files, and writes all test commands into your project's `CLAUDE.md` — so the TDD skills need no manual setup.
Running the update script without arguments updates only the skill groups you have installed, including skills newly added to them, instead of installing every group. Name a group to add it.
The `commit` skill's setup shows an example commit message for every option, so you pick the style, body, granularity, issue references, and attribution by how your commits will look.
The `commit` skill asks before putting several changes into one commit, and splits a file that mixes two changes into separate commits instead of filing it under one.

added.en: The `commit` skill releases too: ask it to release and it proposes the next version from the unreleased changes, then makes one release commit that moves them under that version, tags it, and pushes both — or runs your project's own release task when it has one.

New `commit` skill: commits your changes in your project's convention — Conventional Commits, Gitmoji, or plain subjects — asking once per project about message style, body, granularity, issue references, and Claude attribution, and optionally keeping a translated `CHANGELOG.json` for the audiences you pick or describe.
The install and update scripts take skill group names (`tdd`, `craft-review`, `commit`) to install or update only those groups.
Running the install script without arguments shows a checklist of skill groups to pick from (arrow keys move, space selects, enter confirms) instead of installing everything.

New `engineering-rules` skill: sets up the checks your code must pass — static analysis, security scanning, testing strategy, enforcement in hooks and CI, accessibility, performance budgets, and logging conventions. It detects your stacks, researches freely usable tools for each, lets you pick tools and rulesets (strictest recommended), and wires every check as a task, offering to set up mise when the project doesn't use it.

changed.en: The green phase checks that everything it added is actually run by a test — unused lines and branches get reverted instead of shipped.
Every construct in a green change must trace to a failing assertion. Faking a value to pass is allowed; the next test is what forces it to generalise.
A faked value is pinned down on the following slice, and a behaviour boundary always gets two slices, one on each side.
When mutation testing finds a survivor in batch code, the fix goes into the loop rather than a one-off patch.
The refactor phase no longer adds new behaviour, even when it looks necessary.

added.en: TDD loop — builds a feature one behaviour at a time in batches of five, each batch closed by a refactor pass and a mutation-testing pass, pausing for your review. Red, green, and refactor each run in isolation so no imagined implementation leaks between phases.
Red, green, and refactor phases usable on their own: write one failing test, make it pass with the smallest change, or improve a design without touching behaviour.

Craft review — reviews a change through five independent lenses (Domain-Driven Design, Code Smells, Clean Code, Pragmatic Programmer, Philosophy of Software Design), reported separately with no lens overriding another. Its findings drive the TDD loop's refactor pass.
